title: How to Dehumidify a Room (With or Without a Dehumidifier)
h1: How to Dehumidify a Room — With or Without a Dehumidifier
dek: Clammy air, foggy windows, a musty smell? Here's how to dry out a room fast, plus the free fixes that keep it dry.
description: How to dehumidify a room: set up a dehumidifier the right way, or reduce humidity without one using fans, AC, ventilation, absorbers and leak fixes.
intro: Humid rooms feel sticky, smell musty and invite mold, dust mites and pests. Learning **how to dehumidify a room** comes down to two jobs: removing the moisture already in the air, and stopping new moisture from building up. A dehumidifier is the fastest way to do the first. Ventilation, air conditioning and a few habit changes handle the second — and can often make a real difference even if you don't own a dehumidifier.
The target is simple: keep indoor relative humidity between 30% and 50%, as the EPA recommends, and never let it sit above 60%. A $15 hygrometer tells you where you stand.

Below, we cover how to dehumidify a room with a dehumidifier, ten ways to reduce humidity without one, what homemade dehumidifiers can and can't do, and quick tips for bathrooms, basements, garages and cars.

sections.heading: How to dehumidify a room with a dehumidifier

items: **Size it right.** A bedroom or office usually needs about 20 pints; a large or very damp room 35–50.
**Close the room.** Shut windows and doors so you're drying that room, not the outdoors or the rest of the house.
**Place it well.** Put it near the center of the room, several inches from walls and furniture. See [where to place a dehumidifier](/guides/where-to-place-a-dehumidifier/).
**Set a target.** Choose 45–50% rather than continuous mode.
**Drain continuously if possible.** A hose to a floor drain or a pump model keeps it running.
**Keep it clean.** Wash the filter every couple of weeks in heavy use.

blocks.text: In a closed, humid room, most dehumidifiers bring humidity down noticeably within a few hours. If yours runs constantly without reaching the target, it may be undersized or moisture may be entering faster than it can remove it.

sections.heading: How to dehumidify a room without a dehumidifier

items.label: Run exhaust fans
items.text: Use the bathroom fan during showers and for about 20 minutes afterward, and a range hood vented outdoors when cooking.

items.label: Use the air conditioner
items.text: AC removes moisture as it cools. Our [dehumidifier vs. air conditioner](/guides/dehumidifier-vs-air-conditioner/) guide explains when that's enough.

items.label: Ventilate when it's drier outside
items.text: Opening windows helps only when outdoor air is drier. Compare dew points, not just humidity percentages; a cool, dry day is ideal.

items.label: Fix leaks and drainage
items.text: Repair dripping pipes, insulate sweating cold-water lines, clean gutters and direct downspouts away from the house.

items.label: Dry laundry outside or in a vented dryer
items.text: A rack of wet clothes releases a lot of moisture indoors. Make sure the dryer vents outdoors.

items.label: Take shorter, cooler showers
items.text: Less steam means less moisture to remove.

items.label: Move houseplants and cover water
items.text: Plants, aquariums and simmering pots all add moisture. Group plants elsewhere and cover tanks.

items.label: Keep air moving
items.text: Ceiling and box fans help surfaces dry and stop damp pockets in corners and closets.

items.label: Use moisture absorbers in small spaces
items.text: Calcium chloride tubs or silica packs work in closets and cabinets. See our [best moisture absorber](/best/best-moisture-absorber/) picks.

items.label: Warm cold rooms
items.text: In cool weather, gentle heat lowers relative humidity and reduces condensation, though it doesn't remove moisture.

blocks.text: A popular DIY dehumidifier is a bucket of calcium chloride or rock salt that pulls moisture from the air. These can help in a small, closed space like a closet, but they absorb far less than an electric dehumidifier and need regular refilling.

blocks.title: Reality check
blocks.text: A damp room can hold far more water than a homemade absorber can capture. If the room stays above 60%, it needs a real dehumidifier or a moisture source fix.

Run a properly vented exhaust fan, wipe down wet surfaces and leave the door open after showers. Windowless bathrooms may need a compact unit; see our [best dehumidifier for bathroom](/best/best-dehumidifier-for-bathroom/) guide.

Fix gutters and grading, insulate cold-water pipes, and run a 35–50 pint unit with continuous drainage. Our [best dehumidifier for basement](/best/best-dehumidifier-for-basement/) picks cover the options.
How to dehumidify a garage or crawl space

Seal gaps and keep wet vehicles and gear from dripping inside. Crawl spaces usually need a vapor barrier plus a dedicated unit; see our [crawl space dehumidifier installation](/guides/crawl-space-dehumidifier-installation/) guide.
Run the AC with fresh air, dry wet mats and use a renewable silica pack. See our [best car dehumidifier](/best/best-car-dehumidifier/) guide.

To dehumidify a room, measure first, then remove moisture and stop it at the source. A right-sized dehumidifier set to 45–50% is the fastest fix, while exhaust fans, AC, smart ventilation and leak repairs can lower humidity without one. Homemade absorbers help only in small, closed spaces. Not sure whether you need a machine? See [when to use a dehumidifier](/guides/when-to-use-a-dehumidifier/).

faqs.q: How can I dehumidify a room fast?
faqs.a: Close the doors and windows, run a right-sized dehumidifier on its highest setting until the room reaches about 50%, and use a fan to keep air moving. Running the AC also helps.

faqs.q: How do I reduce humidity in my house without a dehumidifier?
faqs.a: Use exhaust fans in bathrooms and the kitchen, run the air conditioner, fix leaks, dry laundry outdoors or in a vented dryer, and open windows only when outdoor air is drier than indoor air.
Only when the outdoor air is drier. On a humid summer day, opening windows can make a room more humid. Compare indoor and outdoor dew points before you ventilate.

faqs.q: Do bowls of salt or rice dehumidify a room?
faqs.a: Not meaningfully. Salt and rice absorb only small amounts of moisture. Calcium chloride works better but is best suited to closets and cabinets.

faqs.q: What humidity should a room be?
faqs.a: The EPA recommends keeping indoor humidity between 30% and 50%, and below 60% to limit mold. Many people find 40–50% most comfortable.

faqs.q: How do I dehumidify a room for sleeping?
faqs.a: Run a quiet dehumidifier or the AC in the evening to bring the room to about 45–50%, then let the humidistat cycle overnight. See our [best dehumidifier for bedroom](/best/best-dehumidifier-for-bedroom/) picks.
